title: Three cards, one red face
hook: You draw a card and see red. The other side: red or blue?

knows: probability as a fraction of equally likely cases
doesNotKnow: that "which card" and "which face" are different lists of cases
that the clue (a red face is up) is about faces

misconception: You see red, so the card is red/red or red/blue, so the hidden side is red half the time.
objective: The learner can explain that a red face up is equally likely to be any of the three red faces, two of which belong to the red/red card, so the hidden side is red 2/3 of the time.
keyState: Only the three red faces kept, then each turned over: 2 of 3 backs are red.

claims.text: With a random card and a random side up, each of the six faces is equally likely to land up.
claims.source: Card chosen with chance 1/3, side with chance 1/2, independently: each face 1/6 (model assumption in src/demos/probability/three-cards-one-red-face/model.ts).

claims.text: Three of the six faces are red, and two of those belong to the red/red card, so a red face up hides a red back 2/3 of the time.
claims.source: Enumeration of the six faces (exact() in model.ts): red faces = red/red side 1, red/red side 2, red/blue side 1; backs red, red, blue.

claims.text: The stage's draws are seeded: in the first 60, red was up 23 times with a red back 18 times (78%); over 600 draws, 212 of 310 (68%).
claims.source: draws() in model.ts, mulberry32 seed 1889, untuned (the first seed tried). Over seeds 1-500, the red-back share in 60 draws had middle 95% 50%-83% (median 68%). The reveal quotes only the learner's own tally.

recall.question: A bag has a coin with heads on both sides and a normal coin. You pick one at random, toss it, and see heads. How likely is the other side heads?
recall.why: There are three heads faces that could be up; two belong to the double-headed coin, whose other side is heads. Count faces, not coins: 2/3.
